Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM)
DC recognizes the importance of STEM as part of a well-rounded educational experience. STEM skills and knowledge are not only valuable components to a solid academic program, but also core fundamentals for life experience. STEM skills and knowledge help students develop logic, problem-solving, and critical thinking skills that can be used in every discipline and that enable them to compete in the continually growing high-tech job sector. As such, DC strives to improve STEM opportunities for all its students and has established the following statewide goals for STEM:
Goal 1: To prepare all students in DC to graduate high school with a college- and career-ready mastery of math, science, engineering and technology
Goal 2: To increase the number of DC students who major in STEM fields in college and enter STEM careers

title: Introduction to EDUC 219
text:
The course addresses the philosophy, history, and sociology of American education, particularly with regard to the role of diversity in the development and operation of the nation’s education system. Particular attention will be paid to major social, political, and economic forces that have shaped and continue to shape American schools and educational practices.
Additionally, the course is designed to build among pre-service teachers a global awareness of how racial, cultural, linguistic, gender, income, and ability diversity affect educational opportunity. This course will enable candidates to discern the extent to which some forms of teaching and learning enhance democratic ideals while others do not, and to begin developing a professional identity that reflects the ideals of equal access and social justice.

text:
This module examines education in the colonial period and the Early Republic. We will consider Indigenous education, colonial schooling, slavery, literacy, religion, family and community learning, and the early development of public education in the United States.
The module asks students to examine how education and schooling were shaped by colonization, race, power, labor, citizenship, religion, and economic development. We will also consider how Black communities, Indigenous communities, and other groups created, protected, and advanced educational practices and institutions under conditions of exclusion and constraint.

title: Module 3: Whole Number Operations
text:
Discussion of Properties

Commutative Property
The order of addition or multiplication does not affect the result:
\(a + b = b + a\)
\(a \times b = b \times a\)



Associative Property
Changing grouping does not affect the sum or product:
\((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\)
\((a \times b) \times c = a \times (b \times c)\)



Distributive Property
Multiplication distributes over addition:
\(a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c\)



Identity Property
Adding zero or multiplying by one leaves the number unchanged:
\(a + 0 = a\)
\(a \times 1 = a\)



Zero Property of Multiplication
Multiplying any number by zero results in zero:
\(a \times 0 = 0\)

Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA)
The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) process is an instructional approach in mathematics that helps students develop a deeper understanding of mathematical concepts by progressing through three stages:

Concrete Stage:


Students use physical, hands-on objects to model mathematical concepts
Examples include base-10 blocks, counters, fraction bars, or algebra tiles
This stage allows students to manipulate tangible objects to solve problems




Image from CRA methods by the Mathematics Initiative at www.pattan.net



Representational (or Pictorial) Stage:


Students transition to using visual representations of the concrete objects
This may involve drawings, diagrams, or other pictorial models
Examples include number lines, bar models, or sketches of manipulatives




Image from CRA methods by the Mathematics Initiative at www.pattan.net



Abstract Stage:


Students work with abstract symbols and notation
This includes numbers, variables, and mathematical symbols (+, -, x, ÷)
Students apply their understanding to solve problems using standard algorithms




Image from CRA methods by the Mathematics Initiative at www.pattan.net


The CRA approach deepens mathematical understanding and help students internalize abstract concepts by first grounding them in concrete experiences.

title: Module 3: Whole Number Operations
text:
Teaching Exponents
Pattern Blocks
Pattern blocks can be used to visually demonstrate exponents. For example:

Use one triangle to represent \(1 \times 1\)
Four triangles together represent \(2 \times 2\)
Nine triangles together represent \(3 \times 3\)


Draw the pattern for \(4 \times 4\) and \(5 \times 5\).
These patterns helps students visualize the quantity of exponents but we want to also show them representations of exponents as repeated multiplication; we can use base-ten blocks to extend their understanding.
Base Ten Blocks
Base ten blocks work well for teaching powers of 10:

A unit cube represents \(10^0 = (1)\)
A rod represents \(10^1 = 10 = (10)\)
A flat represents \(10^2 = 10 x 10 = (100)\)
A large cube represents \(10^3 = 10 x 10 x 10 = (1000)\)

Grid Paper
Grid paper allows students to draw squares and rectangles to represent exponents:

A \(2 x 2\) square represents \(2^2\)
A \(3 x 3\) square represents \(3^2\)
A \(2 x 2 x 2\) cube represents \(2^3\)


Draw the figures representing \(3^3\) and \(4^2\).

title: Module 3: Whole Number Operations
text:
Teaching Roots
Algebra Tiles
Algebra tiles are also good for teaching square roots:

Use the square tiles to build perfect square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, etc.)
The side length of the square represents the square root

For example, a \(3x3\) square of tiles has an area of \(9\), so the square root of \(9\) is \(3\).
Grid Paper
Grid paper can be used to estimate non-perfect square roots:

Draw a square with the given area (e.g. 17)
Count the side length to estimate the square root
Refine by adding partial squares

This provides a visual model for estimating irrational square roots.

Number Lines
Use a number line to place square roots between perfect squares:

Mark perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, etc.)
Estimate locations of other square roots between them

This helps students understand square roots as numbers between integers.
We can use manipulatives to build conceptual understanding before moving to procedures. Allow students to explore and discover patterns through hands-on activities. Gradually connect the concrete models to symbolic notation as students gain understanding.

title: Module 6: Progressive and Vocational Education
text:
This module examines Progressive Era and vocational approaches to education, including the ways reformers, policymakers, educators, and communities debated the purposes of schooling in a rapidly changing society. We will consider how industrialization, urbanization, immigration, race, class, gender, disability, and changing labor conditions shaped educational reform.
The module asks students to examine both the promises and limits of progressive and vocational education. Educational reform can expand access, support inquiry, connect schools to community life, and create new opportunities. At the same time, reform can reproduce social hierarchies when it sorts students into unequal pathways, defines some forms of knowledge as more valuable than others, or restricts access to rigorous intellectual and civic learning.

title: Module 4: Common Schools, Expansion, and Exclusion
text:
This module examines the nineteenth-century expansion of common schools and the unequal educational systems that developed alongside them. We will study the common-school movement, immigration, urbanization, normal schools, teacher preparation, and the growing role of states and local communities in public education.
The module also emphasizes exclusion. As public schooling expanded, access was not distributed equally. Race, class, gender, disability, language, religion, immigration status, geography, and political power shaped who could enter schools, what kinds of schools they attended, what they were taught, and the resources available to them.

title: Course overview
text:
Course focus
EDUC 219 examines the philosophy, history, and sociology of American education, with particular attention to the ways diversity shapes the development and operation of the nation’s education system. We will study social, political, and economic forces that have shaped American schools and educational opportunity, while considering how racial, cultural, linguistic, gender, income, and ability diversity affect teaching and learning.
Our work connects historical evidence, educational theory, and professional practice. Across the term, we will explore the relationship between schooling, democratic ideals, equal access, and social justice.

title: Course overview
text:
Course description
The course addresses the philosophy, history, and sociology of American education, particularly with regard to the role of diversity in the development and operation of the nation’s education system. Particular attention will be paid to major social, political, and economic forces that have shaped and continue to shape American schools and educational practices.
Additionally, the course is designed to build among pre-service teachers a global awareness of how racial, cultural, linguistic, gender, income, and ability diversity affect educational opportunity. This course will enable candidates to:

Discern the extent to which some forms of teaching and learning enhance democratic ideals while others do not.
Begin to develop a professional identity that reflects the ideals of equal access and social justice.

title: Course overview
text:
Course objectives
Upon successfully completing the course, you will be able to:

Explore social, political, and economic theories and research that distinguish multiculturalism, diversity, and social justice constructs that have shaped and continue to shape American schools and educational practices.
Contrast the ideal of education and the reality of schooling in America for children from diverse racial, cultural, and linguistic backgrounds by exploring theories and research on stereotypes, prejudice, discrimination, the dynamics of power and privilege, and interlocking systems of oppression that affect teaching and learning.
Explain the historical roots and trajectories of prejudice in the United States and integrate culturally relevant education into curriculum and/or practice.
Develop learning experiences informed by the personal, social, cultural, and historical contexts of students and their communities.
Demonstrate evidence of a professional identity that challenges the status quo and reflects agency regarding the education of African American and other diverse students.

title: Course overview
text:
Course learning sequence
The course moves from broad historical and philosophical inquiry toward collaborative case-based research and trial reenactment.

Historical inquiry and timelines: Students define criteria for historical significance, select historical bookend events, locate two primary-source artifacts, construct physical timelines, and contribute records to a shared digital timeline/database. The class database will identify whether an item is classified as a major event and whether it is directly related to education.
Archival research and trial groups: Students connect historical documents, events, and educational contexts to a selected Plessy v. Ferguson or Brown v. Board of Education trial group. Trial-group discussion posts and research will support the development of historical context, evidence, arguments, competing perspectives, and trial materials.
Personal philosophy of education: Each student will produce a final individual philosophy of education. This is not a philosophy of teaching. It should articulate the student’s developing understanding of the purposes of education and the relationships among schools, democracy, access, diversity, power, and social justice.
Supreme Court trial reenactments: Working in groups, students will research, prepare, and present reenactments of Plessy v. Ferguson and Brown v. Board of Education, attending to historical context, legal claims, competing perspectives, and implications for educational opportunity and justice.

title: Brown v. Board of Education

Historical context
Brown v. Board of Education emerged from a long history of racial segregation in American public life and schooling. For decades, the “separate but equal” doctrine associated with Plessy v. Ferguson allowed states and local communities to maintain racially segregated public institutions.

It consolidated five cases from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, and the District of Columbia that challenged racial segregation in public education. The plaintiffs and their families challenged systems that required Black children to attend separate schools, often under unequal conditions.
The litigation was part of a broader legal strategy developed by the NAACP and its Legal Defense and Educational Fund. Lawyers, families, community members, educators, and civil-rights organizations worked over many years to challenge unequal educational conditions and the constitutional basis of segregation.

The following year, in Brown II, the Court addressed implementation and directed school authorities to begin desegregation with “all deliberate speed.”

text:

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
Historical context
The case emerged during the post-Reconstruction era, when African American civil and political rights were being restricted through state law, local practices, racial violence, and the expanding Jim Crow system. In 1890, Louisiana passed the Separate Car Act, requiring railway companies operating within the state to provide separate accommodations for white and Black passengers.
In 1892, Homer Plessy, a New Orleans resident who was classified as Black under Louisiana law, deliberately sat in a train car designated for white passengers. The action was organized with the support of the Comité des Citoyens, a New Orleans civil-rights organization challenging segregation. Plessy was arrested after refusing to leave the car. His legal challenge eventually reached the United States Supreme Court.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
Constitutional questions
The case asked students, lawyers, judges, and the public to consider several connected questions:

Did Louisiana’s Separate Car Act violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?
Did segregation in public accommodations create an unconstitutional system of racial inequality?
Did the law violate the Thirteenth Amendment’s prohibition on slavery and involuntary servitude?
What authority did states have to regulate public accommodations and racial separation?
Can legal equality exist when social institutions are organized by racial separation?

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
The Court’s decision
On May 18, 1896, the Supreme Court upheld Louisiana’s Separate Car Act. Justice Henry Billings Brown wrote for the majority. The Court concluded that the Fourteenth Amendment was intended to establish legal equality, but it held that laws requiring racial separation did not necessarily imply the legal inferiority of Black Americans. The decision became associated with the doctrine of “separate but equal.”
Justice John Marshall Harlan wrote the lone dissent. He argued that the Constitution is “color-blind” and does not recognize a class system among citizens. His dissent rejected the idea that the state could constitutionally impose racial separation in public life.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
Educational significance
Although the case directly concerned railroad travel rather than schools, its legal logic became a major basis for racial segregation across public life. The decision provided legal justification for segregated public facilities, including transportation, parks, theaters, hospitals, and schools. It shaped the legal and institutional conditions under which unequal school systems were maintained and challenged for decades.
For EDUC 219, the case raises questions about how laws, courts, public institutions, and educational systems can shape unequal access and opportunity. It also provides essential historical and legal context for understanding the litigation strategy and constitutional reasoning later associated with Brown v. Board of Education.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
Trial-group research questions
As you prepare the reenactment, consider:

What were the historical conditions of Reconstruction, disfranchisement, racial violence, and Jim Crow that shaped the case?
How should the Separate Car Act be understood from the perspectives of Homer Plessy, Louisiana officials, railway companies, Black communities, and white supporters of segregation?
What legal arguments could be made under the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments?
What evidence would supporters and opponents of the law use?
How did the Court distinguish legal equality from social equality?
How did the decision influence schools and other institutions of public life?
What are the limits of reenactment? How can the group accurately represent historical arguments without endorsing them?

Carter G. Woodson was a historian, educator, author, and founder of important institutions dedicated to the study of Black history. He is often called the “Father of Black History” because of his work documenting, preserving, and teaching African American history.
Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History and established Negro History Week, which later became Black History Month. His work challenged schools, scholars, and the public to take seriously the histories, intellectual traditions, institutions, and contributions of Black people in the United States.
Dr. Woodson will serve as one of many examples to guide our questions about historical thinking, archives, schooling, and education in American society. Please watch the video below to help frame your historical analysis and archival research assignment.

Creative Methods in Mathematics Teaching



Note


Engaging students in mathematics requires innovative approaches that make abstract concepts tangible and exciting.



Examples of Creative Teaching Methods:

Math Storytelling: Integrate mathematical concepts into narratives.

Example: “The Great Shape Adventure” - a story where geometric shapes are characters solving problems.

Gamification: Turn math lessons into games.

Example: “Fraction Bingo” or “Multiplication Race”

Hands-on Manipulatives: Use physical objects to represent mathematical concepts.

Example: Using Lego bricks for addition and subtraction

Real-world Applications: Connect math to everyday situations.

Example: Planning a class party budget

Technology Integration: Use interactive apps and software.

Example: Geogebra for geometry exploration

title: Module 5: Lesson planning and assessment
text:
Organizing Standards and Lesson Activities



Note


Effective lesson planning aligns standards with engaging activities and clear learning objectives.



Steps for Organizing a Math Lesson:

Identify the Standard:

Example: CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.3.NF.A.1 - Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts.

Set Clear Objectives:

Example: “By the end of the lesson, students will be able to represent and explain fractions using visual models.”

Plan Engaging Activities:

Opening: Fraction scavenger hunt in the classroom
Main Activity: Creating fraction art with colored paper
Closure: Peer teaching of fraction concepts

Incorporate Multiple Representations:

Visual: Fraction circles and number lines
Kinesthetic: Folding paper to show fractions
Symbolic: Writing fractions in numeric form

Differentiation Strategies:

Provide fraction tiles for struggling students
Challenge advanced students with equivalent fractions

Effective assessment in mathematics goes beyond traditional testing, especially in preparation for high-stakes exams.

Formative Assessment Techniques:

Exit tickets: Quick problem-solving at lesson’s end

Digital polls: Real-time feedback on concept understanding

Performance-Based Assessments:

Math projects: Design a playground using geometric shapes
Math journals: Students explain their problem-solving process

Tiered assignments: Varying complexity levels
Choice boards: Students select from assessment options

Regular practice with standardized question formats
Teaching test-taking strategies (e.g., eliminating wrong answers)
Stress-reduction techniques for test anxiety

Adaptive online quizzes
Virtual manipulatives in digital assessments

title: Module 5: Reconstruction and the Law
text:
This module examines Reconstruction as a period of major political, legal, social, and educational transformation following the Civil War. We will consider emancipation, citizenship, the Reconstruction Amendments, Freedmen’s education, the growth of public schooling, and the continuing struggle over who would have access to rights, resources, and educational institutions.
The module emphasizes the relationship between law and schooling. Reconstruction created new possibilities for African American citizenship, political participation, literacy, community institution building, and public education. At the same time, those possibilities were contested and restricted through violence, policy, legal decisions, and the reassertion of white supremacy.

title: Module 2: Philosophies of Education
text:
This module introduces historical traditions and contemporary discourses in philosophies of education. We will examine how philosophical ideas shape beliefs about the purposes of education, the role of schools in democratic society, the relationships among knowledge, learning, teaching, and citizenship, and the distribution of educational opportunity.

text:
Historical artifacts
Historical artifacts and primary sources help us investigate how people, institutions, communities, policies, and events shaped educational experiences. In this course, historical inquiry is not only about identifying facts from the past; it is also about asking how evidence, interpretation, and historical context shape what we understand about schools and society.






Historical thinking


Historical thinking is the practice of using evidence, context, chronology, and interpretation to understand the past and its relationships to the present and future.
Historical thinking asks us to consider why we examine the past in order to better understand the world around us and the world ahead of us. For educators and informed citizens, it helps us interpret institutions, policies, social conditions, and unequal opportunities with greater care.









Primary source


A primary source is material created during the historical period being studied or by someone directly connected to the event, experience, institution, or idea under investigation.
Examples include court opinions, laws, letters, newspaper articles, photographs, speeches, school records, meeting minutes, maps, oral histories, and archival documents.









Historical artifact


A historical artifact is an object, document, image, record, or other source that provides evidence about people, institutions, events, and social life in the past.
For this course, artifacts may directly concern education or may provide broader historical context for understanding schools, law, communities, race, citizenship, and educational opportunity.









Major historical event


A major historical event is an event that meets a stated set of criteria for historical significance.
As part of the timeline activity, your group will develop and apply its own definition. The point is not merely to label an event “important,” but to explain what makes it historically significant, to whom, at what scale, and with what consequences.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Schooling and education
Although people often use the terms interchangeably, education and schooling are not identical.






Education


Education is the broad process through which people develop knowledge, skills, values, identities, relationships, and ways of understanding the world. Education occurs in schools, families, communities, workplaces, religious institutions, cultural organizations, social movements, and everyday life.









Schooling


Schooling refers more specifically to formal, organized educational experiences provided through institutions such as public schools, private schools, colleges, universities, and other credentialing systems.
Schooling includes curriculum, assessment, policies, schedules, rules, professional roles, funding structures, and institutional decisions that shape access to learning.



Questions for discussion

Can a person be educated outside of school?
What do schools provide that other educational settings may not provide?
What kinds of knowledge, histories, identities, and ways of being are recognized or ignored in formal schooling?
When do schooling and education support one another? When might they conflict?

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Diversity
Diversity describes differences among people and communities. In EDUC 219, we will consider how multiple forms of diversity shape educational experience, opportunity, representation, and institutional decision making.






Diversity


Diversity includes differences related to race, ethnicity, culture, language, gender, sexuality, income, religion, nationality, immigration history, disability, ability, family structure, geography, and other social locations.
Diversity is not simply a list of individual characteristics. It also concerns how institutions respond to differences and how social systems distribute recognition, resources, power, and opportunity.



Diversity and educational opportunity
Race, culture, language, gender, income, and ability can shape:

Access to schools, courses, teachers, learning materials, and technology.
How students and families are perceived, categorized, or treated.
Curriculum content and whose histories, languages, knowledge, and experiences are represented.
Discipline, special education, tracking, testing, and other institutional practices.
Students’ experiences of belonging, safety, dignity, participation, and academic opportunity.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Multiculturalism, diversity, and social justice
These terms are related, but they do not mean the same thing.






Multiculturalism


Multiculturalism is an approach that recognizes, studies, and values the histories, cultures, perspectives, and contributions of multiple groups in society.
In education, multicultural approaches may shape curriculum, texts, classroom discussion, school programming, and institutional practices.









Social justice


Social justice concerns the fair distribution of rights, resources, recognition, opportunity, and participation. In education, social justice asks how schools can identify and challenge inequities rather than simply treating unequal conditions as normal or inevitable.









Equity and equality


Equality generally means providing the same resources, rules, or treatment to everyone.
Equity means responding to unequal conditions, barriers, and needs in ways intended to make genuine access, participation, and opportunity possible.
The distinction matters because identical treatment does not always produce fair or equitable outcomes.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Power, privilege, prejudice, and discrimination
Understanding schooling in American society requires attention to how social power operates. Schools do not exist apart from their political, economic, legal, cultural, and historical contexts.






Power


Power is the ability to shape decisions, define what counts as knowledge, distribute resources, establish rules, influence institutions, and affect the conditions of other people’s lives.









Privilege


Privilege refers to unearned advantages or reduced barriers that individuals or groups may experience because of their social position within broader systems of power.









Prejudice


Prejudice is a preconceived judgment, belief, or attitude about a person or group that is not based on adequate knowledge or individual experience.









Discrimination


Discrimination is unequal treatment, exclusion, restriction, or harm directed toward people because of their membership in a social group or because they are perceived to belong to that group.









Systems of oppression


Systems of oppression are interconnected institutional, cultural, legal, economic, and social arrangements that produce and maintain unequal power, resources, recognition, and opportunity across social groups.
In this course, we will examine how such systems affect schooling, teaching, learning, policy, access, and educational outcomes.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Educational opportunity
Educational opportunity is more than simply being enrolled in a school. It concerns whether students have meaningful access to high-quality learning conditions, relationships, resources, curriculum, participation, and pathways.






Equal access


Equal access refers to the principle that students should not be excluded from educational opportunities because of race, culture, language, gender, income, ability, disability, or other social characteristics.
Questions about equal access include who can enter schools, courses, programs, activities, and decision-making spaces, as well as what supports are necessary for meaningful participation.



Questions for discussion

What should count as an educational opportunity?
Can separate institutions be equal in practice?
How do funding, transportation, housing, curriculum, discipline, testing, and teacher assignment shape access?
What responsibilities do educators, policymakers, courts, families, and communities have for creating equitable educational conditions?

Starting questions
A philosophy of education is not simply a list of preferred classroom activities or a philosophy of teaching. It is an argument about the purposes, values, obligations, and possibilities of education.
As you begin drafting your philosophy of education, consider:

What purposes should schools serve in a democratic society?
How have historical struggles over racial, cultural, linguistic, gender, income, and ability diversity shaped my understanding of education?
What is the relationship among equal access, justice, democracy, and teaching?
How should educators respond to unequal histories and present educational conditions?
What kind of professional identity and agency do I want to develop?







Philosophy of education


Your final individual philosophy of education should communicate your developing understanding of the purposes of education and the relationships among schools, democracy, access, diversity, power, and social justice.
It is not a philosophy of teaching. Your work should move beyond preferred instructional strategies to address the broader purposes and responsibilities of education.

The historical thinking, archival research, documentation, and philosophical questions introduced in this module will support that work. Trial groups will use historical evidence to build context, analyze arguments, represent competing perspectives, and consider the educational consequences of Supreme Court decisions.






Start building connections


As you encounter an event, artifact, concept, or course reading, ask:

Does this help explain the historical context of Plessy or Brown?
Does it illuminate questions about segregation, citizenship, public institutions, schooling, or equal access?
Could it become a source, claim, question, or piece of evidence for a trial group?

Equity means responding to unequal conditions, barriers, and needs in ways intended to make genuine access, participation, and opportunity possible.
The distinction matters because identical treatment does not always produce fair or equitable outcomes.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Power, privilege, prejudice, and discrimination
Understanding schooling in American society requires attention to how social power operates. Schools do not exist apart from their political, economic, legal, cultural, and historical contexts.






Power



Power is the ability to shape decisions, define what counts as knowledge, distribute resources, establish rules, influence institutions, and affect the conditions of other people’s lives.








Privilege



Privilege refers to unearned advantages or reduced barriers that individuals or groups may experience because of their social position within broader systems of power.








Prejudice



Prejudice is a preconceived judgment, belief, or attitude about a person or group that is not based on adequate knowledge or individual experience.








Discrimination



Discrimination is unequal treatment, exclusion, restriction, or harm directed toward people because of their membership in a social group or because they are perceived to belong to that group.








Systems of oppression



Systems of oppression are interconnected institutional, cultural, legal, economic, and social arrangements that produce and maintain unequal power, resources, recognition, and opportunity across social groups.
In this course, we will examine how such systems affect schooling, teaching, learning, policy, access, and educational outcomes.

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Educational opportunity
Educational opportunity is more than simply being enrolled in a school. It concerns whether students have meaningful access to high-quality learning conditions, relationships, resources, curriculum, participation, and pathways.






Equal access



Equal access refers to the principle that students should not be excluded from educational opportunities because of race, culture, language, gender, income, ability, disability, or other social characteristics.
Questions about equal access include who can enter schools, courses, programs, activities, and decision-making spaces, as well as what supports are necessary for meaningful participation.



Questions for discussion

What should count as an educational opportunity?
Can separate institutions be equal in practice?
How do funding, transportation, housing, curriculum, discipline, testing, and teacher assignment shape access?
What responsibilities do educators, policymakers, courts, families, and communities have for creating equitable educational conditions?

title: Module 1: Schooling for Diverse Populations in American Society
text:
Starting questions
A philosophy of education is not simply a list of preferred classroom activities or a philosophy of teaching. It is an argument about the purposes, values, obligations, and possibilities of education.
As you begin drafting your philosophy of education, consider:

What purposes should schools serve in a democratic society?
How have historical struggles over racial, cultural, linguistic, gender, income, and ability diversity shaped my understanding of education?
What is the relationship among equal access, justice, democracy, and teaching?
How should educators respond to unequal histories and present educational conditions?
What kind of professional identity and agency do I want to develop?







Philosophy of education



Your final individual philosophy of education should communicate your developing understanding of the purposes of education and the relationships among schools, democracy, access, diversity, power, and social justice.
It is not a philosophy of teaching. Your work should move beyond preferred instructional strategies to address the broader purposes and responsibilities of education.

title: Module 6: Progressive and Vocational Education
text:
This module examines Progressive Era and vocational approaches to education, including the ways reformers, policymakers, educators, and communities debated the purposes of schooling in a rapidly changing society. We will consider how industrialization, urbanization, immigration, race, class, gender, disability, and changing labor conditions shaped educational reform.
The module asks students to examine both the promises and limits of progressive and vocational education. Educational reform can expand access, support inquiry, connect schools to community life, and create new opportunities. At the same time, reform can reproduce social hierarchies when it sorts students into unequal pathways, defines some forms of knowledge as more valuable than others, or restricts access to rigorous intellectual and civic learning.

title: Module 5: Reconstruction and the Law
text:
This module examines Reconstruction as a period of major political, legal, social, and educational transformation following the Civil War. We will consider emancipation, citizenship, the Reconstruction Amendments, Freedmen’s education, the growth of public schooling, and the continuing struggle over who would have access to rights, resources, and educational institutions.
The module emphasizes the relationship between law and schooling. Reconstruction created new possibilities for African American citizenship, political participation, literacy, community institution building, and public education. At the same time, those possibilities were contested and restricted through violence, policy, legal decisions, and the reassertion of white supremacy.
